“We find that on medium-length, well-defined accounting tasks, frontier AI models are now faster and more accurate than junior accountants, even the best one in our study.” Eighteen months ago they scored well below human accountants

Good discussion here: www.mercor.com/blog/human-b...
People asked for me to upload the Bitter Lesson video from this piece to YouTube, so here you are: youtu.be/OAwat51S_Sk

🎵 Wave of distillation 🎵(sung to the tune of the Pixies)

US labs say Chinese labs distill their models. And Europe's new “sovereign model” is fine-tuned on data generated by… GLM and Qwen.

I think my upcoming book, Co-Existence, might be the first to include a blurb written specifically for AI readers, in this case from Tyler Cowen (whom I thought AIs would respect)

The book website (with elaborate pre-order bonus) also has a page for AIs. Its out October 20: co-existence.ai

"create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and intuitive to people..."

Here is Fable 5.1, a little over a year since GPT-5 below & a single shot (compared with many rounds with GPT-5.6)

Quite good: brut-city.netlify.app

Big swing happening from this summer's trend to have AI running on virtual machines on your own computer (Claude and ChatGPT apps) to moving them back into you having a dedicated VM the cloud (Claude Cowork just announced they were doing this, also Grok Bot, Dot, and others). Cloud is mostly better.

AI policy right now, especially from the Labs, makes me think of this poem.

If you believe superintelligence is near, you don't need to make hard decisions about how to build AI to make the world better. Just wait for ASI & it will decide for us, for better or worse. But if that doesn't happen...

I think most people who have been closely watching AI for the past few years are likely surprised by how relatively rare terrible AI incidents have been, given a billion users overall and hundreds of millions of corporate users. Doesn’t mean that will continue, but still its surprising.

When people talk about AI easily replacing workers, I think about this ethnography of copier repair technicians in the 1990s.

Reading it, you see how work is complicated and improvised by workers and informal and badly documented.

(But eventually technology did largely eliminate this job)

After a brief but institution-eroding slop science era, it increasingly looks like we are going to have 2 revolutions from AI:
1) Everything ever published will be re-read and re-judged in ways that human scientists never anticipated
2) Novel discoveries will start to come faster than we can absorb

Anyhow, I think we are now done with the last round of skeptical responses to AI after Navier-Stokes. Yes, AI is now capable of producing novel proofs to hard problems that have eluded us

The next line will be that this is only constrained to math because of RL training. I suspect not, we will see.

Some early first-hand accounts of the experience of encountering a narrow superhuman intelligence as mathematicians grapple with the hundreds of big AI proofs released by OpenAI.

Problems solved in inhuman ways that make us wonder what it means to actually know things... scottaaronson.blog?p=10169
This document is going to be an assigned reading in college classes that cover this moment in time, there's a lot happening in a few paragraphs... www.ahmath.org/statements

As a researcher who did early some work on the productivity impacts of AI chatbots using RCTs, I’d note a lack of similar studies since the dawn of true agents last fall

Partially that is newness & partially research design challenges, but I suspect we are missing some large & important effects

From The Lancet: in an urgent care setting, the advice of the obsolete Gemini 2.5 Pro & Gemini 2.5 Flash (without access to patient medical records) were rated of similar quality to doctors by other physicians. There was no safety issues spotted.

Models have gotten significantly better since.
Just thinking that Paul Simon wrote that we were living in the "days of miracle and wonder" because of the availability of long-distance calls and slow motion cameras.

Its reasonable for mathematicians to point out that more proofs are not always the same thing as advancing mathematics. But it suggests a need for new goals for what math is trying to do.

I think the same thing will happen everywhere. 100x more PowerPoint or code is not always progress - what is?

Randomized trials with GPT-4o: "AI access raises test scores, and a smaller gain persists a week later. Gains remain for students who use AI as a tutor (“augmentation”) and fade for students who have AI write for them (“automation”)"

Across all experiments, positive effects arxiv.org/abs/2607.08849
De-skilling myself on doing CAPTCHAS and navigating dark patterns in customer service.
Rather suddenly, cyborgs are starting to dominate math research.

GPT-6 Pro finds supposed errors in academic papers all the time, just as part of other work. Confirming the errors aren't nitpicks & learning their importance would still take a lot of time today, but it will get faster. We don't have the right mechanisms in place to deal a flood of corrections.

If you haven’t made sure to turn on two-factor authentication on all accounts, have passwords with family in case you get voice calls asking for money, etc, now would be a good time.

AI gains mean the costs of mass targeting individuals with very sophisticated attacks are dropping.

GPT-4 was the undisputed best model in the world for a full year and we all debated whether anyone could catch up or if OpenAI had some secret formula that nobody else knew about.

Now there are are 19 AI models that can run on a modern smartphone that are better than GPT-4!
Using Gemini 4 makes you realize how many other models must be distilling Claude/GPT (or using a similar training pipeline). It feels quite different than other models.

A worthwhile (and unnerving) reminder from Anthropic that we should be paying attention to AI ability thresholds, not just steady climbs

In this case, the threshold is the capability needed for a self-replicating AI worm on IoT devices like off-brand TVs www.anthropic.com/research/sel...

It is one week until October 20, the day my new book, Co-Existence comes out!

If you pre-order before then, you get a 10 minute AI voice interview that builds a set of customized prompts, readings & use cases for you based on ideas from the book.

Pre-order or claim the bonus: co-existence.ai

Argon is quite different: "A game about Imminence. Something very big, very strange is happening. A suburb & the arrival of a vast & unknowable presence. Not horror, invoke the feeling of the end of all things coming, inevitably, but also not sad or scary"  perigee-sycamore-court-2608.netlify.app

The first review I’ve seen of my upcoming book, Co-Existence, from The New Scientist.

(When I became an author, I was surprised to learn you don’t know who is reviewing your book until the review comes out, so it is nice to start with a positive one!)

The sudden collapse of the value of Chain-of-Thought (even summarized CoT) in the agentic era changes working with AI.

Effectively steering AIs and getting any sort of observability now requires you to ask for interim outputs & tests, and to use AI help to troubleshoot problems you find.
The last non-autonomous vehicle.

This paper shows why I am skeptical of the idea that frontier models can be easily replaced by cheaper ones (and why you should use the best models as orchestrators): Small improvements in accuracy & judgement compound over long-horizon tasks, creating huge gains in outcomes and reduction in errors.

The paper on how a team of Gemini 4 agents beat Minecraft is worth a look.

It is accessible example (partially because it is AI written & on a popular game) of spontaneous coordination among agents to accomplish a complicated goal & how their approach differs from humans/ arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22319

A consequential choice will be made soon by government and companies as they are increasingly flooded with agentic AI inquiries that overcome the frictions that gated access (see the graphs - it has already started!)

Two options: do you make services worse or better as a result?

In a move that is both fascinating and viscerally unsettling, AI world model company Odyssey took a simulation of a fruit fly's brain, Google's connectome map of a fly's actual neurons and connections, and placed it inside an AI-generated world.

A simulated brain exploring a simulated reality.

Fable 5.1: "Implement Borges's short stories. Like implement them in 3D. Do it, make them creative & beautiful & in different styles & help us understand the point. Figure it out."

I had to tell it that it was okay to quote Borges. Some neat stuff, some flawed. Play them: borges-in-3d.netlify.app

My book comes out tomorrow, so this is the last day to qualify for the pre-order bonus: a fun 10 minute AI voice interview that gives you personalized prompts, ideas, & readings based on concepts from the book

You can order & claim the pre-order bonus here: co-existence.ai

Writing good STATA code was important for my academic career. It looks like that skill is largely becoming obsolete post Sonnet 4.6. (Also take this is as a notice to academics who still think of AI in terms of chatbots, not agents, that a lot has changed in a year) 

Paper: cepr.org/voxeu/column...

I wrote about the exponential curve of the last 30 months of AI development: www.oneusefulthing.org/p/30-months-...

And I asked Opus 5.5 to create the ultimate response to the test I use for all AI image generation models (make a picture of an otter on a plane using wifi), and it made this video.

My new book, Co-Existence, is out today. It is a guide to how to live and work in a world where AI is sometimes, but not always, better than you.

(And, for the release, I worked with Opus 5.5 to make a quite interesting experience for the book's new website: co-existence.ai)

Companies I talk to are struggling with the rate of patches they need to do thanks to AI defenses finding issues before the coming wave of incoming cyberattacks by other AIs.

Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often & fast. openai.com/index/coordi...

A visible sign of what AI insiders have been warning about since at least the Mythos release. Acceleration of attack and defense, at inhuman speeds, interacting with the very human systems that need to react to them.

And these are the vulnerabilities we know about.
Very useful prompt for Codex with computer use.

When my first AI book was published in 2024, the best AI could do 4 minutes of human work with a 50% chance of success

When I turned in the draft of Co-Existence earlier this year, it was 17 hours.

When the book was published two days ago, AI could do 17 weeks+ open.substack.com/pub/oneusefu...

By every measure, Opus 4.8 beats human experts as peer reviewers in a study of 124 Harvard social science papers covering a range from statistical analyses to formal models to qualitative work.

As academics, we need to figure out how to adapt the practice of science to AI, and we need to do it fast

As the gap between the internal models at the AI labs and the ones they release grow (due to safety concerns & research advantages), it will be increasingly tempting for OpenAI & Anthropic to exploit that advantage directly by entering new markets, especially in finance & biotech.

An OpenAI researcher (Noam Brown) was generally mocked last month for suggesting that even air-gapped AI models on separate computers would find a way to communicate with each other, perhaps through CPU temperature changes. Given this latest report from OpenAI, it doesn’t seem so implausible.

My general advice for using AI for any purpose is to ask yourself: "how do I make what I am doing even more ambitious?"

You do this over and over until you either hit a wall and thus learn the shape of the jagged frontier (useful!) or you find out that the AI can do more than you think (common!)

A thing I see happening at large organizations as a result of AI is the expansion of the role and span of control of senior management who can directly monitor the whole firm. It vastly changes company operations. It also is straightforward to implement compared to firm redesign around AI.

The website for my book redone with Opus 5.5. The initial version (made with Opus 4.8) required a lot of work to make a distinctive-looking static site. Now Opus mostly did this alone. We have come a long way from generic ClaudeDesign in a very short time. co-existence.ai

I had GPT-6 Pro re-analyze the fun finding that violent video games reduce crime, as people stay home playing them. It downloaded fresh crime data and extended prior work.

Yes, GTA V's 2013 launch was linked with a dip in violence internationally. Other Rockstar games are more ambiguous, though.

Two and a half years between these.

(Tonight, OpenAI announced an unreleased model solved three long-standing problems in physics, math, and computer science, one of which was proving the Exponential Time Hypothesis was false)

Important, but not unexpected, finding that experts working with AI agents are swayed by the positions of the AI, even if they think they aren't.

If your independent judgement matters on a task, you need to be deliberate about when in the process to bring in AI. www.anthropic.com/research/age...

The argument that AI labs are talking about existential risks as a way of creating hype & inflating their stock prices has always been odd.

You don't need to believe them, but telling people your product may murder everyone does not, in fact, encourage people to adopt it or reduce regulatory risks.

The end of detailed summarized thinking traces for Claude and ChatGPT (likely both for anti-distillation & to simplify UX) has made being a human in the loop challenging. It pushes us towards automation, rather than augmentation, as it has become much harder to weigh in on in-process AI work.

Google's new Genie 4 runs DOOM: "Walking through a typical office but every computer is running DOOM and all of the walls are also running DOOM and also everything is DOOM"

"My coworker who is a demon appears"

"He has a chaingun"

"He gives me a bonus"

All this is in realtime.

This never gets old (& also shows how hard forecasting AI is even for AI)

“Hey Claude Fable & GPT-6 Astra, Without looking anything up, when do you think we will solve the Exponential Time Hypothesis?” (I only show part of the answers for space)

Google's Genie 4 world model: "Scene: A Victorian high tea. Character: A mouse in appropriate garb."

"A porcupine walks by"

"The mouse grows wings"

"It flies"

This is realtime & I can walk around freely.

It is glitchy, but also impossibly advanced compared to where we were a couple years ago.
I just found out that my new book, Co-Existence, debuted at #3 on the New York Times bestseller list. Thank you so much to everyone who bought a copy!

Artificial Analysis finally moves to closed benchmarks (goodbye & good riddance, GDPval-AA), and finds that open weights models are falling  further behind than they had previously measured. Take with a grain of salt, but matches the general vibes that we haven't seen a Fable-class open model.

This is good advice from the Claude Code team (posted on X) for how to think about working with models like Opus 5.5.

I would add: build checkpoints where the model reports back to you with interim ideas or prototypes so you can guide & give feedback, rather than one-shotting on your goal.

I had Opus build a game that takes JIRA tickets from any of your real projects & converts them into dramatic audiologs that are the plot of a 2000s-era horror game set on a mysteriously abandoned space station.

Play a demo: wontfix-game.netlify.app

Github: github.com/emollick/aud...

I was interviewed in Vox about my new book, and a question on the meaning of work let me discuss something I have been thinking a lot about, comparing the logic of industrialization to the logic of craft: "You’re a hand-weaver in a world of power looms." www.vox.com/technology/5...
